content.thinking:
I'll design a whimsical capybara roughly 1.2m long with an exaggerated rounded barrel body and blunt head, topped with a small songbird about 0.1m tall, writing the whole module carefully in one pass since I can't test it incrementally, watching out for unused variables and API misuse.

Mapping out the skeleton...

Adding jaw joint with aim target, then sketching a tail stub as a single joint off the hips. Now I'm setting up the four legs using the limb helper, defining hip positions, foot targets, segment lengths, and bend directions for the knees.

For the front legs with 2 lengths totaling 0.34, three joint names work out to shoulder, elbow, wrist, and the distance from hip height to target checks out fine. I'm settling on a side naming convention where positive x maps to "L" and negative to "R", matching world coordinate conventions rather than local head framing. Legs parent off the spine joints or hips appropriately, and now I need to figure out how the chain consumes the limb point arrays to build each joint.

I'm sweeping tapered radii along each leg to get capybara's stubby thick limbs with fur-painted color, then adding toes as small rods or capsule segments at the foot tip—four toes up front, three in back—while keeping the foot low enough to just touch or slightly sink into the floor within the allowed tolerance.

Adding toe claws as small capsules with dark coloring, binding them to the leg's tip joint. Now thinking through the body loft path across hips, spine, and neck bones, and worrying about duplicate stations where chains share a starting joint.

I'm sketching chubby capybara-style body cross-sections along the spine—widths, heights, and vertical offsets at each z-station to get a deep, rounded barrel shape.

Looking at proportions, the resulting body height seems too tall for a capybara (which sits closer to the ground with less belly clearance), so I need to compress the vertical dimensions and lower the centerline a bit to match a realistic ~0.5m back height.

I'm recalculating leg lengths against the hip-to-ground distance to keep feet grounded, and redefining the spine and hip joint positions to match the new, lower body centerline.

Now I'm shaping the head with a blunt capybara-like skull and snout, placing the nose and head size, then plotting the body's cross-section stations along its length—width and height at each point to form the chubby, whimsical silhouette.

For the legs, I'm computing hip and foot targets for front and rear limbs with appropriate segment lengths and bend directions so the IK chains reach the ground plausibly, checking distances against total leg length and figuring out which spine joint each leg attaches to.

Now I'm sizing the leg bone radii against the body width to keep them embedded properly, adding a haunch ellipsoid for the rear hip area, and starting to pick capybara fur colors with a tan base and darker back tone.

Building the fur paint function...

I'm simplifying to subtle directional streaking between light and dark coat tones, sized for realistic texel density on a capybara-scale model. For whimsy, I'm thinking of adding a small bird perched on its head and maybe a few tiny flowers, keeping embellishments light rather than overdoing it with full costumes.

Now I'm building the head construction, starting with the skull as a scaled sphere and roughing in the blunt capybara snout shape.

Adjusting snout proportions so the dome cap doesn't overshoot the head length—shortening the path end to around z=0.76 to keep the head length more reasonable relative to the 1.3m body. Adding a dark ellipsoid nose near the snout tip, positioned slightly toward the top since capybaras have nostrils on top of the snout.

Adjusting the snout and jaw geometry so the upper snout sits higher and bulkier to properly overlap the lower jaw without gaps, then considering adding a subtle mouth line or smile curve between them for definition.

I'll drape the snout sweep path onto the surface so points pull toward the nearest geometry, then give it a thin dark sweep radius. For the eyes, I'm going for bigger glossy whimsical spheres placed on the sides of the skull, so I'm working out the skull ellipsoid's center and radii to position them correctly near the top.

Checking the eye position against the skull ellipsoid equation confirms it sits right on the surface, so I'll place a dark brown eye sphere there with a small white highlight sphere offset toward the outer-forward-upper direction for shine.

For the lazy, whimsical expression I'm adding a partial eyelid using a sphere slice with limited theta length, positioned over the upper portion of the eye in the fur color to give that half-lidded look.

Using flat dark fur color for the lid. Now working on the ears—small rounded capybara ears on the top-back of the head, built as an extruded rounded shape oriented sideways with thickness along the depth axis, figuring out the right orientation vectors so they face correctly.

Still positioning the ears, calculating where the ear outline sits relative to the head's ellipsoid surface so it sits flush against the skull at the correct height and angle.

Checking the x/y axes are perpendicular for the ear orientation, which they are. For whiskers, I'll add a few thin dark rods per side on the snout using low-poly tube segments to keep them minimal. For fur details, I'm considering small tuft cards with an SVG texture for the cheeks.

For the fur card texture, I'll use a simple triangle-ish tuft shape tinted by the coat paint color rather than hardcoding colors, so it blends naturally with the body. I'm scattering around 160-200 of these cards across the body with small leaning sizes to build up a fuzzy coat effect.

Now I'm thinking about the small bird perched on top of the creature's head — a chubby, round songbird like a whimsical bluebird with maybe a warm-colored chest, sitting at the skull's crown, roughly 11cm long, and I need to work out its basic skeleton structure next.

Working out bird placement on the skull: feet resting around y 0.53, body centered near y 0.585 with small ellipsoid radii, head forward with a tiny beak cone, and a whimsical crest plus small black eye spheres for character.

Now I'm shaping the wings with a teardrop outline extruded along each side of the body, pointed sharply backward with a few defined corner points for a stylized feather silhouette.

Writing wing paint thresholds...

Now I'm shaping the tapered tail extrude pointing back and slightly up from the body, working out a non-perpendicular x-axis direction that should still work for the extrude orientation even if not perfectly orthogonal to y.

Still shaping tail outline... I'll add a countershaded belly for the bird body, with a lighter underside contrasting the main color.

Adding pink blush spheres, then working out eye placement with dark spheres and white highlights positioned on the head sphere's surface. I'm also placing tiny orange leg rods from the body to the feet with small toes, and figuring out the skull ellipsoid's position and radii near the top of the head.

Adjusting the bird's body center upward so the legs don't sink into the head — settling on a centre y of 0.595 with legs running from 0.552 to 0.532, short and orange, with toes resting against the skull top.

Now I'm working out the head placement intersecting slightly with the body front, eyes just above the beak, and a beak tip extending forward and up. I'm adding a three-spike crest at the top of the head angled back, positioning the wings at their own small offset, and figuring out the tail placement extending backward from the body so it doesn't collide with the skull's back edge.

Now I'm defining the bird's joint hierarchy: a body joint parenting the head joint, with the head aiming slightly up and back, a jaw joint for the beak parented to the head for upper and lower beak pieces, and wing joints parented to the body angled outward and back for the armature bones.

Still adding joints for tail and legs, and planning to assign parts to bones explicitly by nearest joint rather than relying on automatic assignment, keeping the head joint as the parent so the bird rides properly on the capybara's head.

Verifying the cheek position lands right on the skull surface, I adjust the ellipsoid scale slightly so it protrudes just enough. Now I'm adding the capybara's signature dark morrillo gland patch as an oval bump on top of the snout.

Placing the dark morrillo at the snout top, I set its position and radii, then define a tapered snout path with a radius function shrinking toward the nose, capped by a rounded dome, plus a separate dark nose pad sphere near the tip.

Adding the nostrils as small pinkish spheres sunk into the front of the dome, then settling on a darker color for them. For the snout coloring I'm using a countershade function to blend a darker brown top with a lighter underside, and similarly setting up the head paint as a warm countershade variant of the body coat.

Now I'm working out the daisy flower accessory near the right ear, positioning its center and arranging petals as small spheres placed around it in a ring, computing each petal's angle and offset in the plane facing outward from the head.

Checking the skull geometry at z=0.5, I find the ear region wider, so I'll place the flower near the ear base on the right side at roughly [-0.083, 0.495, 0.535], checking it sits against the skull surface there.

To avoid overlapping the ear outline, I'll shift the ear slightly back to z=0.48 and move the flower forward to z=0.55, recomputing the surface x-coordinate to confirm the flower still rests against the skull at approximately [-0.085, 0.497, 0.55].

Checking clearances: the eye at z=0.62 with radius 0.03 reaches 0.59, while the flower petals extend to 0.576, so there's a thin but acceptable gap. I'm satisfied the legs and feet sit properly on the floor given the model's height and allowed sink tolerance, so now I'm moving on to painting gradient fur coloring on the legs, darker toward the lower portions.

Writing leg paint gradients...

The body-to-neck transition for the capybara needs no distinct neck since the loft covers up to the head region, so I'm checking that the body's final loft station properly meets the skull's back position without a gap.

Checking that the rounded end cap on the last body station doesn't pop out wider than the head — I'm adjusting the station dimensions so the dome narrows fast enough to stay tucked inside the head's width instead of making it look embedded or oversized.

I'm placing a small tail nub sphere near the rump cap tip around z -0.73 to -0.76, widening the rear haunch station for a rounder rump, and starting to lay out the rear body stations with their widths and heights.

Continuing the spine stations through the hips and front body, checking bottom clearance for legs, and verifying the catmull spine path connects smoothly through the chain. I'm also sizing haunch ellipsoids so they poke slightly outside the body width at z -0.45 for a chubbier look.

Writing SVG fur tuft texture...

For scatter parameters, I'm setting card sizes, lean angles, and counts for body fur versus skull fur, with a filter so hits facing downward don't get cards. I'm also planning whiskers, eyelashes, a chin tuft, and capybara-style orange front incisors near the snout's lower edge.

I'm positioning small tooth boxes at the jaw tip, checking the dome geometry of the snout so the teeth sit correctly where the upper lip curve meets the mouth front.

Now I'm shaping the lower jaw as a shorter rounded path than the upper snout, colored cream, then adding a drape line along the mouth using a thin catmull-rom sweep that follows the snout's curvature from the corner to the tip.

Eyelids and blush are settled, eyebrows skipped, and I'm adding a few small feather tufts as a crest on the bird's head for extra character. For the export, I'm defining the scene metadata with name, description, style, and commit hash, then double-checking which helper functions I actually import and use—createBuilder, catmull, limb, countershade, mottle, grain, gradient, paint, svg, rng—trimming out anything unused like vec or frame.

Now I'm working through the limb function's signature—root point, target point, segment lengths, and bend directions per joint—figuring out how to express front leg bends (elbow pointing back) versus rear leg bends (knee forward) as direction arrays passed into the IK builder.

I'm then setting up the chain calls for front and rear legs, matching point arrays to name arrays (three points for front legs, four for rear), and deciding joint parents—spine joint for front limbs, hips for rear—to keep the skeleton hierarchy consistent before building the body loft sweep from hips through spine to neck.

Now I'm working out the toes: writing a helper that places small angled capsules per toe with slight x-offsets per side, keeping their tips near the ground and tucked under the leg's end joint so the feet read naturally when the character stands.

I'm setting up the bird-leg accents next, then adding a tail joint off the hips with a short nub part, and deciding how to handle bone assignment and role naming for the head, jaw, and hips joints so the skeleton hierarchy stays consistent.

Now I'm placing the eyes symmetrically on the head bone, using a dark glossy sphere protruding from the surface, plus a partial-sphere eyelid shape positioned just above each eye socket.

I'm positioning two small highlight spheres on the eye surface to give a glossy catchlight effect, then moving on to define the fur coat paint using a grain function that blends countershading colors.

Defining ear and wing outlines...

Adding spikes for the lower beak attached to the jaw bone, then setting up the jaw joint parented to the head with proper aim and role. I'm placing leg joints with orange rod segments, keeping the daisy riding on the head bone, and double-checking that bone parameters and joint chains all use proper Joint object types.

Now I'm writing the leg loop, building a chain for each side's leg with shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints parented to the spine, then sweeping a tube shape along it with adjusted radii for a tapered limb look.

I'm doing the same for the rear legs with hip, knee, hock, and foot joints, double-checking that all joint names stay unique across front and rear limbs so the chain naming doesn't collide, and confirming the spine has three joints matching the catmull path count.

Now I'm writing a toes helper that spreads four front toes and three rear toes along the x-axis with small rods angling down to the ground, skipping nail details since the toes are already dark brown. Then I'm confirming surface calls on body parts like the head/skull work fine regardless of part creation order.

Checking sweep API types next — making sure the radius function returns a properly typed tuple rather than a generic number array, so I'm annotating it explicitly as a two-number tuple. Gradient point inputs look fine as tuples.

For whiskers, I'm positioning three per side near the snout, computing base coordinates relative to snout curvature at roughly y=0.42, z=0.72-0.76.

Still writing whisker rods...

Then moving to body paint with countershading (blue over cream), skipping chest blush for simplicity, confirming the scatter texture card size and triangle geometry, and setting the seeded RNG with a fixed seed of 7 for consistent placement. Loft colors use the coat, body/neck geometry is already covered by the main loft, and head parts get the head paint color. Finishing up by composing the bird's eyes and head lines, then writing the final output.
